title: Mini-Project 01:Commission to Analyze Taxpayer Spending (CATS)
text:
Introduction

The pay structure of New York City (NYC) is important to ensuring equitable pay and workforce retention while managing the allocation of public funds efficiently. The city happens to be one of the largest municipal employers in the United States employing a total of 354,572 workers across 72 agencies in the 2023 fiscal year (NYC Government, 2023). NYC’s workforce comprises of about 94% fulltime workers and 6% part-time workers. In addition, about 58% of the workforce are female (NYC Government, 2023).The median annual base salary of fulltime workers was estimated at $83,465 excluding overtime and benefits in fiscal year 2023(NYC Government, 2023). The city is noted for spending a significant amount on overtime compensation. Transparency in salary distribution including base pay and overtime compensation is essential for fostering public trust and accountability in government spending. This paper aims to evaluate the implications of proposed policy changes that could reshape NYC’s payroll structure. By analyzing salary trends, overtime expenditures and workforce allocation this report provides data-driven insights to inform decision-making by the CATS Commissioners. The analysis uses payroll data between 2015 and 2024 from New York City Open Database. Each record includes variables such as employee agency, job title, base salary and total overtime paid at the end of the fiscal year (New York City Open Data, 2024). This dataset allows for an in-depth review of payroll distribution and overtime expenditures, helping policymakers understand where budgetary adjustments may be necessary.

Mayor Eric L. Adams Career Salary

Mayor Eric L. Adams’ career and salary history shows a clear progression that reflects his increasing responsibilities in public service. As Brooklyn Borough President, he earned $160,000 in fiscal years 2014 and 2015. In the same role, his salary increased to $179,200 between 2016 and 2021. This reflects periodic adjustments during his time in that role. In 2022, when he became Mayor of New York City, his compensation jumped to $258,750. This has been maintained until 2024. This noticeable salary increases underlines the significant difference in scope and responsibility between managing a single borough and overseeing the entire city, as the mayoral position carries greater administrative and leadership duties. Overall, the table not only tracks the numerical changes in his pay but also illustrates how his career advancement has been accompanied by a corresponding rise in compensation, aligning with the broader expectations and demands of his new role.

Distribution of Total Compensation

The results from the histogram shows that the total compensation is highly right-skewed. The bulk of the data clusters toward the lower end of the total compensation scale with a tall bar in the leftmost bins. This tall bar at the lowest bins signals two things, either there are many zero total compensation in the data which may be an error or there are many low earning workers in NYC municipal. As total compensation increases, the frequency of employees decreases, forming a “long tail” on the right. This indicates that while most employees earn relatively moderate amounts, a smaller subset receives significantly higher compensation. Also, the box plot shows the distribution of total compensation. It’s apparent that the distribution is right-skewed with majority of employees falling within a relatively moderate compensation range while a smaller number receive substantially higher pay. The box plot also shows the presence of outliers in the data. There are a fair number of people earning beyond $300,000. The median salary is $69,492, meaning half of the employees earn less and half earn more. The 10th percentile (p10) is $29,162, indicating that 10% of employees earn below this amount, while the 90th percentile (p90) is $111,839, showing that 10% of employees earn above this value. The 25th percentile (p25) is $44,552, and the 75th percentile (p75) is $92,184, which together represent the middle 50% of salaries.

Task4:Instructor-Provided Questions

The analysis shows that the highest base rate of pay is for the job title “MEMBER, CIVILIAN COMPLAINT REVIEW BOARD” with an average hourly rate of $320. This indicates that the role may require specialized skills and significant responsibility, reflecting the importance and expertise needed to handle complex civil complaint reviews. The data reveals that Gregory P. Russ from NYC Housing holds the record for the single highest city total payroll with his top earning recorded in fiscal year 2022. This same individual had the highest single pay in fiscal years 2021 and 2020. Internicola James, a Correction Officer in Queens, worked the most overtime hours in this dataset, with a total of 3692.9 hours. Also, from the analysis the data shows that the agency with the highest average total annual payroll is the Office of Racial Equity. On average, each employee in this agency earns $151,093 when combining base salary and overtime pay. This indicates that, compared to other agencies, employees in the Office of Racial Equity are paid at a higher rate which could be due to higher base salaries, more overtime or a combination of both. Again, the data shows that the DEPT OF ED PEDAGOGICAL consistently had the highest number of employees on payroll from 2014 to 2024. In 2014, the department employed 100,589 individuals and this number increased to 111,857 in 2015. Although there were some small changes in the following years, the count reached 114,999 by 2020 and peaked at 120,453 in 2022. After the peak in 2022, the employee count fell to 106,882 in 2023 before slightly rising to 108,209 in 2024. The consistently high employee count in the DEPT OF ED PEDAGOGICAL highlights its major role in managing New York City’s public education programs. Results from the analysis shows that the FIRE DEPARTMENT has the highest overtime usage with an average of about 345.89 overtime hours per employee compared to regular hours. This suggests that firefighters often work a significant number of extra hours, likely due to the demanding nature of emergency services and the need to respond to unpredictable situations. The high overtime figure could also indicate staffing challenges or periods of increased workload that require firefighters to extend their shifts. The analysis also reveals that employees working outside the five boroughs earn an average annual salary of $71,983. This lower figure compared to salaries within New York City’s core counties may reflect variations in job roles, budget priorities or local cost of living. Finally, the results indicates that over the past ten years, the city’s total payroll has grown by approximately $6.66 billion, representing a 28.1% increase.

#| code-summary: "Code"
  #defining 10 year period
  last_year <- max(nyc_payroll$fiscal_year, na.rm = TRUE)
  first_year <- last_year - 9 
  
  # Calculate aggregate payroll per year for the 10-year period
  payroll_trend <- nyc_payroll |>
    filter(fiscal_year >= first_year & fiscal_year <= last_year) |>
    group_by(fiscal_year) |>
    summarize(annual_payroll = sum(total_compensation, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(fiscal_year)
  
  # Calculating growth: absolute and percent
  absolute_growth <- payroll_trend$annual_payroll[nrow(payroll_trend)] - payroll_trend$annual_payroll[1]
  percent_growth <- (payroll_trend$annual_payroll[nrow(payroll_trend)] / payroll_trend$annual_payroll[1] - 1) * 100
  
  # View the annual payroll trend and growth results
  print(payroll_trend)

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
A comprehensive analysis of transit system data has led to the proposal of the new GTA IV awards, celebrating transit agencies that excel in environmental performance and efficiency. The awards leverage detailed data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s State Electricity Profiles, the NTD’s 2023 Annual Database Energy Consumption report and the National Transit Database’s Service by Agency report.

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text: Data Aquisition and Description

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text:
Initial Analysis of SEP Data

Which state has the most expensive retail electricity?


Which state has the ‘dirtiest’ electricity mix?


On average, how many pounds of CO2 are emitted per MWh of electricity produced in the US? (Note that you will need to use a suitably weighted average here.)


What is the rarest primary energy source in the US? What is the associated cost of electricity and where is it used?


My home state, Texas, has a reputation as being the home of “dirty fossil fuels” while NY has a reputation as a leader in clean energy. How many times cleaner is NY’s energy mix than that of Texas?

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text:
Data Collection and Description
Data was sourced from the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s (EIA) State Electricity Profiles. The data was obtained by parsing the EIA SEP summary pages using custom code, which converted the raw information into a tidy table format suitable for analysis. The profiles provide detailed state-level insights into electricity generation which is used to estimate the environmental impacts of powering electric transit systems. Importantly, the analysis assumes that electricity generation within a state is fungible—meaning that every transit authority is attributed the same average generation emissions, regardless of any “green supply” agreements they might have. This approach simplifies the comparison of environmental impacts across different transit systems while providing a consistent basis for assessing emissions. In addition to the EIA SEP data, another dataset was obtained from the NTD’s 2023 Annual Database Energy Consumption report as an excel file which provides detailed fuel consumption information for transit agencies. This dataset includes key identifiers such as NTD ID, Mode, and Agency Name, with columns that quantify different type of fuel usage. To streamline the analysis, basic data cleaning was conducted. A key column Mode, was transformed by recoding the Mode column from its original two-letter codes (e.g., HR, DR, MB) to descriptive labels like “Heavy Rail,” “Demand Response” and “Bus”. Lastly,2023 Annual Database Service by Agency report was sourced from the National Transit Database. It provides detailed service-level information for 302 transit agencies across the United States. This dataset includes key variables such as the agency name, city, state, total unlinked passenger trips (UPT) and total passenger miles traveled (MILES), along with a unique numeric identifier (NTD ID) for each agency. Basic data cleaning including converting NTD ID values to numeric format and filtering out records with zero miles were done to ensure the accuracy and usability of the data.

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text:
Distribution CO2 Emissions
The box plot indicates that most U.S. states fall within a moderate range of CO₂ emissions per MWh with the middle 50% of states falling within a relatively narrow range. The median is located near the middle of the box, suggesting that half of the states have CO₂ emissions per MWh below this level and half above. The data is unimodal and has an outlier. Overall, the box plot suggests that most states cluster around a moderate emission level but at least one state has much higher emissions. The histogram provides a clearer picture of the overall distribution. A large number of states cluster toward the lower end of emissions, forming a peak in that region. As emissions increase, the number of states decreases, resulting in a right-skewed pattern. This aligns with the box plot, where the outlier highlights that only a small portion of states reach very high emission levels compared to most others.

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text:
Task 4: Explore NTD Service Data
The results indicate that MTA New York City Transit, operating in Brooklyn, NY, has the highest annual UPT of approximately 2.63 billion unlinked passenger trips recorded. This extremely high number suggests that the MTA handles an enormous volume of transit activity compared to other agencies. The average trip length for MTA NYC is approximately 3.64 miles. This means that, on average, each unlinked passenger trip on the MTA New York City Transit system covers about 3.64 miles. Also, results indicates that the transit service with the longest average trip length in NYC is operated by the “Private Transportation Corporation” in Brooklyn, NY. With an average trip length of 5.23 miles, this service covers longer distances per trip compared to other NYC transit services in the dataset. The analysis also indicates that New Hampshire (NH) has the fewest total public transit miles of 3,749,892 miles traveled. This suggests that compared to other states, NH has a relatively limited public transit network. Finally, the analysis reveals that not all states are represented in the dataset. Specifically, transit data is missing for Arizona (AZ), Arkansas (AR), California (CA), Colorado (CO), Hawaii (HI), Iowa (IA), Kansas (KS), Louisiana (LA), Missouri (MO), Montana (MT), Nebraska (NE), Nevada (NV), New Mexico (NM), North Dakota (ND), Oklahoma (OK), South Dakota (SD), Texas (TX), Utah (UT), and Wyoming (WY). Thus, the NTD Service dataset covers transit services from 31 states while 19 states are missing from the data.


Code
#Which transit service has the most UPT annually?
max_UPT_service <- NTD_SERVICE |> 
  slice_max(UPT, n = 1)
max_UPT_service
#What is the average trip length of a trip on MTA NYC?
mta_nyc<- NTD_SERVICE |> 
  filter(Agency == "MTA New York City Transit")
  
avg_trip_length <- mta_nyc$MILES / mta_nyc$UPT
      avg_trip_length

#Which transit service in NYC has the longest average trip length?(NB: You need to be careful with the City column here. Certain MTA services are officially located in “New York City” while others are located in Brooklyn.)
nyc_services <- NTD_SERVICE |>
        filter(State == "NY" & (City == "New York City" | City == "Brooklyn"))
nyc_services <- nyc_services |>
        mutate(avg_trip_length = MILES / UPT)
max_trip_service <- nyc_services |>
        slice_max(avg_trip_length, n = 1)
        max_trip_service   
#Which state has the fewest total miles travelled by public transit?
state_total_miles <- NTD_SERVICE |>
          group_by(State) |>
          summarize(total_miles = sum(MILES, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
          slice_min(total_miles, n = 1)
          state_total_miles
#Are all states represented in this data? If no, which ones are missing? The state.name and state.abb objects we used above may be useful here.
all_states <- state.abb
states_in_data <- unique(NTD_SERVICE$State)
missing_states <- setdiff(all_states, states_in_data)
missing_states

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text:
Greenest Transit Agency Award
Agency with the lowest emissions per UPT and per passenger mile. Alternativa de Transporte Integrado is awarded the greenest because it shows zero emissions on both metrics.

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text:
Most Emissions Avoided Award
An agency that through its high service volume (high UPT and miles) combined with zero emissions and avoids a significant amount of potential CO₂. Winner. Ann Arbor Area Transportation Authority stands out here, as it reports a high UPT (4.68e6) and high miles meaning that by operating with zero emissions, it avoids what could have been a large CO₂ output relative to its size.

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text:
Efficiency Excellence Award
Recognizes an agency that, despite operating a high-ridership network, manages to maintain an outstanding efficiency record by reporting zero emissions. Ben Franklin Transit have high ridership relative to their service area and maintain zero emissions.

title: GTA IV Announces Winners for the Greenest Public Transit Agencies
text:
Worst Of Award
Highlights the agency with the highest emissions per UPT or per passenger mile among those with sufficient data. Within the filtered group of agencies (those with UPT ≥ 50,000), all agencies have zero emissions based on the current calculations. This suggests that at least among the agencies with calculated emissions, none are performing poorly by these environmental metrics.
